title: Man shot dead by Calgary police: Global TV captures dramatic standoff: [Early Edition]
article: A Calgary police officer shot and killed a blood-soaked, knife- wielding man who rushed at officers responding to a domestic dispute Friday morning.
The shooting happened on the street in front of 279 Queensland Circle S.E., where the man attacked his wife and mother-in-law about an hour and a half earlier.
The tactical team and K-9 officers had just arrived as reinforcements when Harvinder, or Harbinder, Singh Cheema emerged from the house and walked barefoot, down his front yard and into the street.
"A guy stepped out. The police all had their guns drawn and were yelling at him to 'drop it!' but I didn't know what 'it' was," said Cory Hanson, who watched from a few doors down.
Cheema continued toward a group of officers on the street -- raising a knife over his head -- then turning toward some officers on his right when he was shot.
"There was a gunshot, he was on his knees, then he fell and there were police and dogs all around him," Hanson said.
An ambulance under police escort took the man, believed to be in his 30s, to Foothills Medical Centre where he died a few hours later.
A bloodied kitchen knife remained in the street following the shooting, as did a bullhorn police used in an unsuccessful effort to coax the man peacefully from his house.
The chain of events started at about 11:20 a.m. when Cheema's wife and mother-in-law sought help next door.
Cheema's wife, 25, had a head injury, and his 45-year-old mother- in-law was suffering from slash wounds. Both are in stable condition at Foothills.
Their house was surrounded by uniformed police officers, including a Punjabi-speaking officer using a bullhorn to yell instructions to the man inside.
"We tried to contact him numerous times on the phone, we tried yelling, we tried the bullhorn," Duty Insp. Brooke Bishop said at the scene.
Tactical team and K-9 officers were in the process of setting up around the house when Cheema came out, ignoring repeated instructions to drop the knife.
"He looked crazy," said Global TV cameraman Rob Wallace.
Wallace, a 30-year media veteran, went to the scene thinking he'd be filming a routine arrest -- but things took a deadly turn.
"It looked to me that he was going to attack, and then the shot went off," Wallace said.
Wallace's footage has been turned over to police as evidence.
Witness Lee Denham said the man, clad in white traditional dress, fell hard to the ground and moved his arm slightly before being handcuffed by officers.
Denham said the man was aggressive toward the officers and was ordered several times to drop the knife.
"The police were like, 'Drop the knife, drop the knife, drop the knife,' " he said.
The fatal shot was fired by Const. Ian Vernon, a dog handler with the K-9 unit.
"He's shaken. He's very shaken," said Al Koenig, president of the Calgary Police Association.
Koenig described Vernon as "very conscientious and street-wise" and said the police union will ensure he and his family are given support.
The union also provided legal advice to Vernon, though Koenig said it appears the officer was justified in using deadly force.
"Our members are trained to take decisive action if they're threatened or if they're forced to protect other people's lives," Koenig said.

Police are trained to aim for an attacker's centre of mass as the most effective way of stopping an attack -- the notion of shooting to wound or firing a warning shot is a myth inspired by TV cop shows.
"It's a fallacy to believe that we're trained to shoot someone in the arm or the leg -- that won't stop them," Koenig said.
Police said the man was known to police, and officers had been to the house before.
"There was a domestic history there," said Insp. Peter Davison of the major crimes section.
The Calgary police homicide unit will investigate the shooting in accordance with department policies, and forward its findings onto the Crown prosecutor's office.
Hours after the shooting, crime scene specialists converged on the home to collect evidence that will be used in the investigation.
As well, the professional standards section will conduct its own probe to determine if policies and procedures were followed.
Like Koenig, a senior officer briefed on the shooting said it appears the circumstances justify the shooting.

"Based on the information we have so far, we had a situation with an individual who was clearly aggressive . . . toward our officers and didn't give them any choice," Deputy Chief Jim Hornby said. Provincial law dictates deaths resulting from the use of force can be the subject of a fatality inquiry.
